action_trace.summary: Generated 10 interview questions using 5W1H and Socratic techniques to elicit user goals (consistency with modal editors, workflow efficiency), pain points (unnecessary save dialogs, hash regeneration side effects), and acceptance criteria (dirty-flag semantics, setting scope, lifecycle boundaries) grounded in requirement fragments addressing untouched file handling and storage hash behavior.

Interview questions decompose the untouched-file 'dirty' prompt issue using 5W1H and Socratic techniques to elicit user goals (Vim/Emacs parity), pain points (unwanted save prompts), and acceptance criteria (setting scope, data-loss safeguards, integration with existing features). Chain-of-Thought reasoning identifies root cause (file state tracking), affected personas (terminal-heavy developers), and trade-offs (usability vs. safety).

Generated 10 interview questions using 5W1H and Socratic techniques to elicit user goals (eliminating unnecessary save prompts for untouched files), pain points (workflow interruption vs. Vim/Emacs parity), and acceptance criteria (setting-based control, hash preservation logic). Questions decompose the 'dirty file' problem across user personas, lifecycle stages, and system boundaries to ground requirements in measurable outcomes.

End-user requires VSCode to eliminate save prompts for unmodified newly-created files through Vim/Emacs-aligned behavior or configurable setting, reducing workflow friction and aligning with developer expectations in rapid prototyping and automation scenarios.

End-users require VSCode to eliminate dirty-file prompts for untouched newly-created files to align with Vim/Emacs conventions, reduce workflow interruption, and support rapid prototyping scenarios through a configurable dirty-file semantics setting.

VSCode's current dirty-file behavior for untouched newly-created files creates workflow interruptions and misaligns with Vim/Emacs conventions. Business impact: reduced developer productivity, friction in terminal-based workflows, and team onboarding friction. Solution: implement smart dirty-file detection and provide a configurable setting to align with lightweight editor semantics while maintaining flexibility for formal development practices.

EndUser clarification questions addressing scope (terminal vs. UI creation), modification tracking semantics, configuration granularity, interaction with existing VSCode save settings, and disk-persistence boundaries to resolve ambiguities in the dirty-file behavior requirement.

Six clarification questions raised by EndUser to resolve ambiguities in dirty-file semantics: (1) creation vs. open-time scope, (2) state transition triggers, (3) configuration granularity, (4) Vim/Emacs parity definition, (5) empty-file reversion handling, and (6) storage-hash interaction. These questions target conflicting requirement fragments and underspecified pain-point expectations to enable precise SRS definition.

EndUser raises 7 clarification questions addressing setting scope (retroactive vs. prospective), state transitions (dirty flag lifecycle after modification/undo), creation method distinctions (terminal vs. UI), and configuration granularity (global vs. workspace vs. file-type) to resolve ambiguities in the 'not dirty' file feature and align with diverse team workflows.

Confirmed core requirement: VSCode should not mark newly-created empty untouched files as dirty to align with Vim/Emacs and reduce workflow interruption. Refined scope to include both terminal and UI creation, clarified dirty-state transition on first keystroke, and recommended three-level configuration (user/workspace/file-type) to support both rapid prototyping and team-specific workflows.

EndUser confirms newly-created empty files should not be marked dirty (Vim/Emacs alignment); refines setting scope to dual-level (global + file-type), explicit state-transition on first keystroke, and clear boundary between terminal-created and pre-existing empty files. Configuration flexibility across user/workspace/file-type levels is validated as necessary to support heterogeneous team workflows.

EndUser confirms newly-created empty files should not trigger dirty-file prompts (Vim/Emacs alignment), refines configuration to dual-level scope (global + file-type overrides), and clarifies state-transition logic (dirty on first keystroke, not save action) to balance UX improvement with modification tracking.

Consolidated 7 structured interview records (ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 compliant) addressing VSCode dirty-file behavior for newly-created empty files. Core requirements: (1) eliminate save prompts for untouched new files via terminal/UI (aligns Vim/Emacs), (2) dual-scope configuration (global + file-type), (3) explicit state-transition on first keystroke. Clarifications resolved: creation method distinction, perpetual-clean prevention, scope boundaries. MoSCoW prioritization applied: 4 MUST (functional/behavioral/boundary), 3 SHOULD (config scope/tracking/UX). Enduser pain points (workflow interruption, rapid prototyping friction) directly mapped to requirements; deployer considerations identified for implementation.

Six prioritized user requirements synthesized from interview records and end-user feedback addressing dirty-file semantics for newly-created empty files in VSCode 2026Q3. MUST requirements (4) enforce terminal/UI parity, exclude pre-existing files, and mandate first-keystroke state transition. SHOULD requirements (2) enable dual-scope configuration and preserve post-creation tracking. All requirements trace to confirmed pain points (workflow interruption, rapid prototyping friction) and align with Vim/Emacs industry standards.

Deployer dialogue probes infrastructure persistence layer changes, security/audit implications of bypassing save prompts, scalability of dual-scope configuration matching, deployment strategy (opt-in vs. default-on), telemetry for state-transition tracking, autosave conflict resolution, and extension integration behavior to ensure the 'not dirty' setting is operationally viable and backward-compatible.

Targeted deployment-focused questions probe infrastructure constraints (state tracking at scale, storage/configuration integration), security mandates (audit logging, compliance), scalability across multi-root/remote workspaces, backward-compatibility with extensions, platform-specific file-detection mechanisms, and observability requirements for the dual-scope dirty-file setting feature.

Eight targeted questions probe VSCode's file-state persistence architecture, security implications of creation-method detection, scalability of dual-scope configuration, first-keystroke transition reliability, backward compatibility, observability/telemetry requirements, configuration storage strategy, and edge-case handling—anchoring deployer input to infrastructure constraints, security mandates, and scalability expectations for the dirty-file behavior feature.

Deployer confirms infrastructure readiness: minimal memory overhead, FS-event integration via existing APIs, security compliance with settings isolation, and scalability to 10K+ files. Operational procedures mandate setting-scope hierarchy validation, phased rollout with feature flags, and rollback strategy. Cost-neutral client-side implementation with availability constraints on startup/open latency. Recommend dual-scope configuration (global + file-type overrides) with telemetry-driven rollout across Insiders→Stable pipeline (Q3→Q4 2026).

Infrastructure and operational deployment for dirty-file behavior control requires minimal new resources: integrate state-transition logic into existing keystroke handlers and file-system listeners; implement dual-scope settings (user/workspace/file-type) via settings.json schema extension; enforce <10ms evaluation latency and <5MB memory footprint; validate cross-workspace isolation and state-transition atomicity; no new persistent storage or external dependencies required.

Deployer confirms infrastructure constraints (FS event integration, 5MB in-memory cap, <50ms state-transition latency), security mandates (settings isolation, regex validation), scalability targets (10K+ file support), and operational procedures (state-transition logging, dual-scope configuration defaults, graceful degradation) for VSCode dirty-file behavior control feature. Availability and cost-performance trade-offs favor minimal overhead with backward-compatible fallback behavior.

Deployer requires clarification on 6 critical operational gaps: (1) file-system event integration architecture, (2) memory scalability for large workspaces, (3) security isolation model for dual-scope settings, (4) keystroke detection CPU overhead, (5) file-type override precedence logic, (6) extension API backward compatibility. Chain-of-Thought analysis reveals infrastructure constraints are specified but integration points with existing VSCode systems and conflict-resolution strategies for multi-scope configuration remain underspecified per ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 deployment checklist.

Deployer requires clarification on infrastructure integration (FS event listeners vs. polling), memory/persistence trade-offs for dual-scope configuration, security isolation model for settings inheritance, deployment sequencing relative to existing dirty-tracking subsystem, observability/telemetry requirements, and backward compatibility strategy to ensure reliable implementation of first-keystroke dirty-state transition logic across heterogeneous team workflows.

Deployer requires clarification on five operational dimensions: (1) FS event-listener integration precision for first-keystroke detection; (2) memory budget validation for dual-scope configuration at scale; (3) security isolation guarantees for settings inheritance chain; (4) state-transition trigger semantics (synthetic vs. user input); (5) cost-performance trade-off for file-type override lookup in large workspaces. All clarifications are grounded in deployer_questions and infrastructure constraints (5MB memory cap, FS API integration, settings.json/workspace.json isolation).

Deployer confirms infrastructure feasibility: dirty-file state-transition logic integrates with existing VSCode FS event listeners (chokidar/native APIs) within 5MB memory constraint per workspace; dual-scope configuration (user/workspace-level + file-type overrides) leverages settings.json/workspace.json inheritance with cross-workspace isolation enforced; first-keystroke detection via onDidChangeTextDocument avoids polling overhead; scope boundary (newly-created empty files only) validated against pre-existing file exclusion; precedence and timing clarifications pending confirmation.

Deployer validation confirms infrastructure feasibility: dirty-file state-transition detection integrates with existing VSCode FS event listeners (no polling); dual-scope configuration (user/workspace/file-type) leverages settings.json/workspace.json with enforced cross-workspace isolation; 5MB in-memory footprint per workspace meets cost-performance trade-off. Refine: clarify first-keystroke hook point and file-type override precedence logic. Ready for implementation with phased rollout and telemetry.

Deployer confirms infrastructure integration feasibility: dirty-file state-transition detection via existing VSCode event listeners (chokidar + editor.onDidChangeTextDocument), 5MB per-workspace in-memory storage via file-handle metadata, dual-scope configuration (user/workspace-level + file-type overrides) leveraging settings.json/workspace.json with cross-workspace isolation enforcement. Refine state-transition hook to editor text-change events (not file-system events) for accurate first-keystroke detection. Default to opt-in behavior for backward compatibility. Deployment ready per ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 security and scalability constraints.

Operating environment for vscode_2026q3 dirty-file feature requires standard development workstations (x86-64, 8GB+ RAM, SSD) running Windows 10+, macOS 10.15+, or Linux with native file-system APIs; state tracking integrates with existing VSCode file-system event listeners (chokidar/native FS) with <5MB per-workspace memory footprint; dual-scope configuration (user/workspace-level + file-type overrides) persisted via settings.json/workspace.json with cross-workspace isolation enforced; no specialized hardware, external services, or regulatory compliance beyond VSCode baseline required.
